name: agent-desktop
description: Computer use CLI for AI agents
readme_content:
# agent-desktop Computer use for AI agents: see and operate desktop apps on macOS, Windows, and Linux through the OS accessibility tree.

agent-desktop gives an AI agent computer use without screenshots or pixel matching. It reads the accessibility tree of a desktop app and returns it as JSON, with a ref for every element the agent can act on. The agent clicks or types on a ref, reads the UI again to check the result, and repeats. The loop lives in your agent; agent-desktop has no model inside. It ships as a CLI and a C library. Snapshots, clipboard reads, screenshots, command output, and debug artifacts can contain private desktop content. Keep them out of public logs and uploads. ## Install ```bash npm install -g agent-desktop agent-desktop status # platform, permissions, supported surfaces agent-desktop permissions --guide # macOS: walks you through the Accessibility grant ``` Bun, Yarn and pnpm can install the same package. It includes native binaries and platform helpers for x64 and ARM64. For direct execution without a JavaScript launcher, download the matching native archive from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop/releases) and keep its helper beside the executable. On macOS and Linux, Homebrew also works: `brew install agent-desktop`. There is no official Scoop package yet. The repository no longer maintains a custom Homebrew tap or Scoop bucket. Release archives and building from source are covered in [Installation](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/installation). ## Quick start ```bash agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # interactive elements, each with a ref agent-desktop click @s8f3k2p9:e8 # act on a ref from that snapshot agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i # observe again to verify ``` Each command prints one JSON envelope. A trimmed snapshot: ```json { "version": "2.6", "ok": true, "command": "snapshot", "data": { "app": "Finder", "snapshot_id": "s8f3k2p9", "ref_count": 59, "complete": true, "tree": { "role": "window", "name": "Downloads", "children": [ { "role": "treeitem", "name": "Documents", "ref_id": "@s8f3k2p9:e8", "available_actions": ["Click"] } ] } } } ``` - **Refs belong to their snapshot.** A bare `@e8` is rejected with `INVALID_ARGS`. When the UI changes, an action returns `STALE_REF` or `AMBIGUOUS_TARGET`: take a new snapshot and use its refs. - **Several windows** give `AMBIGUOUS_TARGET`; `snapshot` lists the candidate window ids in `error.details`. Pass one with `--window-id`. - **Dense apps:** map first with `snapshot --skeleton --app Slack -i --compact`, then drill into one region with `snapshot --root @s8f3k2p9:e3 -i --compact`. - **Headless by default.** Ref actions use the accessibility API without moving the pointer or taking focus. The global `--headed` flag allows physical input. - **Post-action waits** observe the ref's original process. Window-owned refs stay pinned to their original window, including refs captured from a sheet, alert, popover, focused view, or Linux menu. macOS application menus keep their application-owned surface and need no document window. The wait reads the whole pinned window, so overlay selectors share its scope. [Wait scope and results](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/configuration#post-action-wait-flags) describe the selector limits. - `type`, `set-value`, and `clipboard-set` accept `--stdin` for piped text, keeping it out of process arguments. Run secret steps as separate commands; batch JSON text appears in process arguments. - **PowerShell.** Quote every ref (`'@s8f3k2p9:e8'`), because a bare `@token` is the splatting operator. The full walkthrough is in the [quick start](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/quick-start). ## How it works Your agent calls the CLI, or the C library in process. Both run the same core, which reaches the OS only through `PlatformAdapter`. Each binary is built for one OS and talks to that OS's accessibility API. ## For AI agents The binary carries guides that match its version: ```bash agent-desktop skills get desktop # the loop, refs, verification and retry rules agent-desktop skills get platform # what differs on the OS you run on agent-desktop --help # flags for one command ``` Install the skill into an agent harness from [skills.sh](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-desktop/agent-desktop): ```bash npx skills add https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop --skill agent-desktop ``` Or add this to your `AGENTS.md`: ```markdown Use `agent-desktop` to see and operate desktop apps. Before the first use, run `agent-desktop skills get desktop` and `agent-desktop skills get platform`, and follow them. ``` Retry a failed command only when `error.disposition.retry` is `safe`. See [JSON output](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/json-output) for the envelope, error codes, and exit codes. ### MCP `agent-desktop mcp` serves every command as an MCP tool over stdio. A tool is named after its command (`desktop_snapshot`, `desktop_click`, `desktop_session_start`), takes that command's arguments, and returns its JSON envelope: ```json { "mcpServers": { "agent-desktop": { "command": "agent-desktop", "args": ["mcp"] } } } ``` Global flags given to `mcp`, such as `--session`, `--headed` or `--trace`, apply to every call. ## Commands agent-desktop has 60 command names, 56 operational commands. The other four (`key-down`, `key-up`, `mouse-down`, `mouse-up`) refuse to run until a daemon can release a held key or button. [Commands](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/commands) documents each one. | Group | Commands | |---|---| | Observe | `snapshot`, `find`, `get`, `is`, `screenshot`, `list-surfaces` | | Act on a ref | `click`, `double-click`, `triple-click`, `right-click`, `type`, `set-value`, `clear`, `focus`, `select`, `toggle`, `check`, `uncheck`, `expand`, `collapse`, `scroll`, `scroll-to` | | Keyboard and mouse | `press`, `hover`, `drag`, `mouse-move`, `mouse-click`, `mouse-wheel`, `key-down`, `key-up`, `mouse-down`, `mouse-up` | | Apps and windows | `launch`, `close-app`, `list-apps`, `list-windows`, `list-displays`, `focus-window`, `resize-window`, `move-window`, `minimize`, `maximize`, `restore`, `open-system-surface` | | Notifications | `list-notifications`, `dismiss-notification`, `dismiss-all-notifications`, `notification-action` | | Clipboard | `clipboard-get`, `clipboard-set`, `clipboard-clear` | | Wait | `wait` | | Sessions | `session`, `trace`, `cursor-overlay` | | System | `status`, `permissions`, `version`, `batch`, `skills` | ## Platform support | Platform | Requirement | Accessibility API | |---|---|---| | [macOS](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/platforms/macos) | macOS 13 or later, Intel or Apple Silicon | AX API | | [Windows](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/platforms/windows) | Windows 10 1809 or later, x64 or ARM64 | UI Automation | | [Linux](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/platforms/linux) | Ubuntu 24.04 or later, x86_64 or aarch64, X11 or Wayland | AT-SPI | Each platform page lists what works headless, what needs `--headed`, and what refuses. ## C library Each release ships `libagent_desktop_ffi`, so a program can call agent-desktop in process. See the [C library docs](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/ffi). ```python import ctypes lib = ctypes.CDLL("./lib/libagent_desktop_ffi.dylib") lib.ad_adapter_create.restype = ctypes.c_void_p lib.ad_adapter_destroy.argtypes = [ctypes.c_void_p] assert lib.ad_init(7) == 0 # AD_RESULT_OK when the header's AD_ABI_VERSION_MAJOR matches the library adapter = lib.ad_adapter_create() lib.ad_adapter_destroy(adapter) ``` ## Development Each platform adapter builds only on its own OS, so scope cargo to the host's packages. On macOS: ```bash HOST_PKGS=(-p agent-desktop-core -p agent-desktop-macos -p agent-desktop -p agent-desktop-ffi) cargo test "${HOST_PKGS[@]}" cargo clippy "${HOST_PKGS[@]}" --all-targets -- -D warnings ``` On Windows, use `agent-desktop-windows` instead of `agent-desktop-macos`; on Linux, `agent-desktop-linux`. [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) lists every gate. ## Documentation - [Introduction](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop): what it is and how it works - [Snapshots and refs](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/snapshots-and-refs) - [Errors and recovery](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/errors-and-recovery) - [Skills](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/skills) - [CONCEPTS.md](CONCEPTS.md): vocabulary - [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md), [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md), [SUPPORT.md](SUPPORT.md) ## License Apache-2.0

Effortless Web Scraping for the Modern Web





Selection methods · Fetchers · Spiders · Proxy Rotation · CLI · MCP

Scrapling is a Python Web Scraping framework that brings fast HTTP requests, stealth browsers, powerful parsing, and concurrent crawling into one library. Scrape static pages, render JavaScript, interact with websites, and extract data from the API calls behind them. Build crawlers with reusable sessions, proxy rotation, automatic retries, pause/resume, and built-in data exports. Use it from Python, the terminal, or your AI agent through its MCP server and Agent Skill. From extracting a few fields to collecting a whole website as clean Markdown, Scrapling covers the full scraping workflow. ## What you can do with Scrapling - **[Fetch & interact](https://scrapling.readthedocs.io/en/latest/fetching/choosing.html)**: Fast HTTP requests, stealth browsers, JavaScript rendering, Cloudflare Turnstile/Interstitial handling, persistent sessions, and background API capture. - **[Parse & extract](https://scrapling.readthedocs.io/en/latest/parsing/selection.html)**: CSS, XPath, text and regex search, adaptive element tracking, similar-element matching, and clean Markdown output. - **[Crawl & export](https://scrapling.readthedocs.io/en/latest/spiders/getting-started.html)**: Concurrent spiders, proxy rotation, retries, AutoThrottle, pause/resume, streaming, ready-made templates, and JSON/JSONL/CSV/XML exports. - **[Scrape with AI or from your terminal](https://scrapling.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ai/mcp-server.html)**: An MCP server for AI agents to browse and extract data, an Agent Skill, CLI commands, and an interactive shell. Start with a single page: ```python from scrapling.fetchers import Fetcher page = Fetcher.get('https://quotes.toscrape.com/') quotes = page.css('.quote .text::text').getall() print(quotes) ``` Or scale up with a spider: ```python from scrapling.spiders import Spider, Response class QuotesSpider(Spider): name = "quotes" start_urls = ["https://quotes.toscrape.com/"] async def parse(self, response: Response): for quote in response.css('.quote'): yield { "text": quote.css('.text::text').get(), "author": quote.css('.author::text').get(), } result = QuotesSpider().start() print(len(result.items)) result.items.to_json("quotes.json") ``` This prints `10` and saves the quotes and authors to `quotes.json`.

name: auto-ontology
description: Auto Ontology is a Python framework for building semantic, graph-based reasoning layers over data. It enables deterministic query generation, better context retrieval, and more explainable AI for LLM and agent workflows.
readme_content:
# Auto Ontology Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability gates agentic analytics: a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong. Agents need a context layer that tells them where data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is an open library that builds that layer from enterprise metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, and exposes it to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. It complements the semantic models customers already own. It enables developers to: - Discover: generate enterprise ontologies from metadata; connect existing ontologies and semantic models; build AI-ready knowledge graphs. - Ground: give agents trusted business meaning for metrics, entities, and relationships; reconcile inconsistent definitions across systems. - Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage; return provenance with every answer. - Expose: serve context to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. Learn: fold certified corrections and usage back into the ontology, so shared context improves with every question. ## Benchmarks To run a text-to-SQL benchmark such as BIRD, refer to the [ontology SQL evaluation repository](https://github.com/NVIDIA/ontology-sql-eval/). > **Licensing & contributions.** Auto Ontology is distributed under the > [Apache License 2.0](./LICENSE). Third-party open-source components > bundled, linked, or otherwise used by this project are listed in > [`THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`](./THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). **This project > is currently not accepting external contributions.**

## Key Features - **Natural-language querying** of structured data — questions are translated to SQL and executed against connected databases, powered by NVIDIA NIM. - **Semantic catalog / ontology layer** over relational sources, stored in Postgres alongside the catalog it describes. - **Authentication & RBAC** —using [Better Auth](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth). - **Web UI** for chat, analysis, data catalog, analytics, and settings. - **Flexible deployment** — Helm chart for Kubernetes or Docker Compose for a local stack. ## Software Components | Component | Technology | Role | Default port | | ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------ | | Frontend | Next.js 16 (React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4), Better Auth, Prisma | Web UI, authentication, API gateway | 3000 | | Backend | FastAPI (Python 3.12+), LangChain | Chat / NL-to-SQL, catalog, datasource APIs | 3001 | | Ingestion worker | FastAPI (Python 3.12+) | Ingests tabular data and writes embeddings | 3002 | | Postgres + pgvector | Relational Database | App metadata, the catalog and ontology, vector store | 5432 | | HashiCorp Vault | Optional | Secure storage of connection credentials | — | ### NVIDIA NIM Auto Ontology uses NVIDIA NIM endpoints for inference — either the hosted [NVIDIA API catalog](https://build.nvidia.com) (`integrate.api.nvidia.com`) or self-hosted NIMs. The defaults in `.env.example` are: - **LLM:** `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b` - **Embeddings:** `nvidia/nemotron-3-embed-1b` - **Reranking:** `nvidia/llama-nemotron-rerank-vl-1b-v2` The endpoints and models are configured via the `DEFAULT_MODELS_ENDPOINT`, `DEFAULT_MODELS_MODEL`, `EMBED_ENDPOINT`, and `EMBED_MODEL` environment variables and require a `DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY`. #### Model triplets Each model role is configured by a **triplet** of environment variables — `_ENDPOINT` (URL), `_API_KEY`, and `_MODEL`: | Prefix | Role | | ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | | `DEFAULT_MODELS` | Shared default; every field below falls back to it. | | `REASONING` | Main chat / NL-to-SQL model. | | `NON_REASONING` | Lighter model used for entity extraction. | | `EMBED` | Text-embedding model (must match between ingest and query). | | `RERANK` | Reranker used by the retrieval flow. | You can set a full triplet, only some of its fields, or none at all — any field left unset falls back to the matching `DEFAULT_MODELS_`. So the simplest setup is to fill in `DEFAULT_MODELS_*` and override per-triplet fields only where they differ (e.g. `EMBED_MODEL`, `NON_REASONING_MODEL`). `*_API_KEY` also falls back to the legacy `NVIDIA_API_KEY` for backward compatibility. ## Quickstart This runs Auto-Ontology with Docker Compose against Wide World Importers, Microsoft's sample sales database. You need Docker with Compose v2, [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), and an NVIDIA API key (`nvapi-...`) from [build.nvidia.com](https://build.nvidia.com). 1. Clone the repository and create `.env`: ```bash git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git && cd auto-ontology cp .env.example .env ``` Then set these values in `.env`: ```dotenv DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY=nvapi-... AUTH_SECRET= APP_URL=http://localhost:3000 POSTGRES_PASSWORD= CONNECTION_STRINGS=postgresql://postgres:@postgres:5432/wideworldimporters AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD= PGADMIN_PASSWORD= ``` Compose publishes Postgres, pgAdmin, and the web app on the host, so replace each default password before you start it. `.env.example` also sets an API key per model role: replace each `nvapi-your-api-key-here` with your key, or delete those lines so they fall back to `DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY`. 2. Start Postgres and load the sample database. The seed script lives in auto-ontology-eval; pass it the Postgres password you set: ```bash docker compose up -d --wait postgres git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology-eval.git ../auto-ontology-eval (cd ../auto-ontology-eval && uv sync && cp .env.example .env && \ POSTGRES_PASSWORD='' \ uv run python scripts/seed/seed_wwi.py --database-name wideworldimporters --drop) ``` 3. Build and start the rest of the stack: ```bash docker compose up -d --build ``` 4. Open and sign in with `AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_EMAIL` and `AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD` from `.env`. Go to **Settings → Semantic Compilation** and turn it on. Ingestion runs at startup; compilation starts immediately and reports **Semantic compilation is ready** when it finishes. 5. Ask a question in **Chat**: > What was revenue for the USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania > in June 2015? The agent resolves *revenue*, *product*, and *state* to terms in the ontology, follows their relationships to the joins it needs, and runs the query. The answer comes back with its SQL and the steps that produced it, so you can check the result against the source: ```text Answer: Revenue for USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania in June 2015 was $588.80, from 3 invoice lines. SQL: SELECT SUM(il.extendedprice) AS revenue, COUNT(*) AS invoice_lines FROM sales.invoicelines il JOIN sales.invoices i ON il.invoiceid = i.invoiceid JOIN warehouse.stockitems si ON il.stockitemid = si.stockitemid JOIN sales.customers c ON i.customerid = c.customerid JOIN application.cities ct ON c.deliverycityid = ct.cityid JOIN application.stateprovinces sp ON ct.stateprovinceid = sp.stateprovinceid WHERE si.stockitemname = 'USB food flash drive - sushi roll' AND sp.stateprovincename = 'Pennsylvania' AND i.invoicedate >= '2015-06-01' AND i.invoicedate < '2015-07-01' Steps: Resolved terms: Invoice Line (revenue), Stock Item, State Province, Invoice Joined: invoice line -> invoice -> customer -> city -> state province Validated the filter values against the data, then executed ``` 6. Ask something the data can't answer. Wide World Importers has no advertising data, so a question about ad spend has nothing to resolve against. An agent connected through [MCP](#mcp-server) checks answerability first and asks you to clarify: ```text You: What was return on ad spend for the sushi roll flash drive in June 2015? Agent: check_answerable -> coverage 0.5; no term covers "ad spend" Agent: I can find revenue for that product, but this data has no advertising spend, so I can't compute return on ad spend. Do you want June 2015 revenue instead, or is ad spend tracked in another source I should connect? ``` If the UI loads without its left navigation after a restart, the browser is holding a stale session cookie. Clear site data for `localhost:3000` and sign in again. For other setup failures, see the [setup skill's troubleshooting guide](./skills/nvidia-ontology-setup/references/troubleshooting.md). ## How it works

Auto-Ontology works in three stages: it generates an ontology, people certify it, and the agent answers questions from it. The ontology holds three kinds of definition: - **Terms.** Business concepts such as *Customer* or *Invoice Line*, each with a description and synonyms, mapped to the columns that hold them. - **SQL attributes.** Reviewed SQL expressions under a term, such as a margin or a rolling total. The agent reuses them, so answers compute each measure the same way. - **Relationships.** How tables join, including bridge tables, inferred from keys and from the data. **Generate.** The ingestion service builds a first draft from the source databases: 1. Read sources: extract schemas, profile columns, and sample values into the catalog. 2. Name entities: extract terms table by table and map each to columns. 3. Resolve relationships: infer joins between tables and bridge tables, and suggest SQL attributes from query history. 4. Write the ontology: store terms, relationships, and SQL attributes in Postgres, with embeddings in pgvector for retrieval. The result is a semantic graph you can explore in the UI. In this example, one compilation of Wide World Importers produced 31 terms; selecting **Order** shows its description, related terms, mapped columns, and SQL attributes:

**Certify.** People make the draft trustworthy: 1. Test with real questions in Chat, or with `check_answerable` and `ask_question` over MCP. 2. Refine terms, descriptions, and SQL attributes in the UI or through the API. 3. Certify names, descriptions, and SQL attributes once they're correct. **Answer.** For each question, the agent: 1. Classifies the intent and extracts the entities the question names. 2. Retrieves candidate terms, columns, and SQL attributes by embedding search. 3. Writes SQL from those

readme_content:
# gstack

gstack turns Claude Code (and other coding agents) into a virtual engineering team: a CEO who rethinks the product, an eng manager who locks architecture, a designer who catches AI slop, a reviewer who finds production bugs, a QA lead who opens a real browser, a security officer who runs OWASP + STRIDE audits, and a release engineer who ships the PR. All slash commands, all Markdown, all free, MIT license.

I'm [Garry Tan](https://x.com/garrytan), President & CEO of [Y Combinator](https://www.ycombinator.com/). This is the open source software factory I use every day, and I'm sharing it because these tools should be available to everyone. The story, the productivity numbers and how I run ten sprints at once are in [Why gstack](docs/why-gstack.md).

Fork it. Improve it. Make it yours. And if you want to hate on free open source software — you're welcome to, but I'd rather you just try it first.

**Who this is for:**
- **Founders and CEOs** — especially technical ones who still want to ship
- **First-time Claude Code users** — structured roles instead of a blank prompt
- **Tech leads and staff engineers** — rigorous review, QA, and release automation on every PR

## Quick start

1. Install gstack (two pastes, about 30 seconds of setup; see below).
2. Run `/office-hours` and describe what you're building. It pushes back on your framing and writes a design doc the other skills read.
3. Run `/review` on any branch with changes. It finds the bugs that pass CI but break in production, and fixes the obvious ones.
4. Run `/qa` on your staging URL, or on an isolated local API, CLI, job or webhook. It opens a real browser, reproduces bugs and fixes them.

Stop there. You'll know if this is for you. When you want the whole sprint, `/autoplan` reviews a plan end to end and `/ship` runs tests, review and the PR.

## Install — about 30 seconds

**Requirements:** [Claude Code](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code), [Git](https://git-scm.com/), [Bun](https://bun.sh/) v1.4.2+ (the tested version; setup refuses Bun older than 1.3.3, which would let compiled tools read a project's `.env`), and [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) on Windows. **Recommended on macOS:** the [Aside](https://aside.com) browser (macOS 15+), which the browser skills, `/make-pdf` and `/diagram` drive first with your real logged-in sessions; without it, `./setup` builds gstack's own bundled browser. `/cso` needs a native toolchain as well; setup says so and leaves it unavailable when the toolchain is absent. Timing, the `/cso` prerequisites and the hooks setup registers: [docs/install.md](docs/install.md).

### Step 1: Install on your machine

Open Claude Code and paste this. Claude does the rest.

> Install gstack: run **`git clone --single-branch --depth 1 https://github.com/garrytan/gstack.git ~/.claude/skills/gstack && cd ~/.claude/skills/gstack && ./setup`** then add a "gstack" section to CLAUDE.md that says to use the /browse skill from gstack for all web browsing and never use mcp\_\_claude-in-chrome\_\_\* tools. Claude Code lists the installed skills itself, so the section needs no skill list. Then ask the user if they also want to add gstack to the current project so teammates get it.

### Step 2: Team mode — auto-update for shared repos (recommended)

From inside your repo, paste this. Switches you to team mode, bootstraps the repo so teammates get gstack automatically, and commits the change:

```bash
(cd ~/.claude/skills/gstack && ./setup --team) && ~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-team-init required && git add .claude/ CLAUDE.md && git commit -m "require gstack for AI-assisted work"
```

No vendored files in your repo, no version drift, no manual upgrades. Every Claude Code session starts with a fast auto-update check (throttled to once/hour, network-failure-safe, completely silent). Team mode follows the `stable` channel: the twice-weekly tagged release (Monday and Thursday, at most once every 72 hours, plus verified security and regression fixes), not every merge to main. `gstack-config set update_channel main` follows every merge instead; see [docs/releases.md](docs/releases.md).

Swap `required` for `optional` if you'd rather nudge teammates than block them.

Team mode's `required` hook runs on Node.js, so every teammate needs Node.js on PATH ([details](docs/install.md#team-mode)). To remove gstack later: [docs/uninstall.md](docs/uninstall.md).

### Other AI Agents

gstack runs on more agents than Claude. Bare `./setup` installs for Claude
Code only (run inside OpenClaw, Hermes or a Dot, it also registers gstack's
skills with that harness: [docs/hosts.md](docs/hosts.md#agent-harnesses)).
Pick another agent with `--host <name>`, or install for every agent setup
detects on this machine with `--host auto`:

```bash
git clone --single-branch --depth 1 https://github.com/garrytan/gstack.git ~/gstack
cd ~/gstack && ./setup --host auto      # or: ./setup --host codex
./setup --status                         # one row per install: host, tier, scope, version, path
```

An explicit `--host X` installs for X only and never changes another agent's
install. `/gstack-upgrade` refreshes every install it registered, one row per
host, and says which ones failed.

Tiers: **full** is certified by a real workflow run (see
[Certify your host](docs/ADDING_A_HOST.md#certify-your-host)); **experimental**
installs and passes the conformance tests but has no certification run yet;
**instruction-only** installs nothing: setup prints what to copy.

| Agent | Tier | Install | First invocation | Safety skills | Outside review needs | Repair |
|-------|------|---------|------------------|---------------|----------------------|--------|
| Claude Code | full | `--host claude` (default) | `/office-hours` | enforced (hooks block) | Codex CLI, signed in | `./setup --host claude` |
| OpenAI Codex CLI | experimental | `--host codex` → `${CODEX_HOME:-~/.codex}/skills/gstack-*/` | ask for `gstack-office-hours` | advisory, not blocked | Claude Code CLI, signed in | `./setup --host codex` |
| OpenCode | experimental | `--host opencode` → `~/.config/opencode/skills/gstack-*/` + `/gstack-*` commands | `/gstack-office-hours` | advisory, not blocked | Codex CLI, signed in | `./setup --host opencode` |
| Cursor | experimental | `--host cursor` → `~/.cursor/skills/gstack-*/` | ask for `gstack-office-hours` | advisory, not blocked | Codex CLI, signed in | `./setup --host cursor` |
| Factory Droid | experimental | `--host factory` → `~/.factory/skills/gstack-*/` | ask for `gstack-office-hours` | advisory, not blocked | Codex CLI, signed in | `./setup --host factory` |
| Kiro | experimental | `--host kiro` → `~/.kiro/skills/gstack-*/` | ask for `gstack-office-hours` | advisory, not blocked | Codex CLI, signed in | `./setup --host kiro` |
| GitHub Copilot CLI | experimental | `--host copilot` → `~/.copilot/skills/gstack-*/` | `/gstack-office-hours` | advisory, not blocked | Codex CLI, signed in | `./setup --host copilot` |
| Antigravity CLI | experimental | `--host agy` (or `--host antigravity`) → `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/skills/gstack-*/` | `/gstack-office-hours` | advisory, not blocked | Codex CLI, signed in | `./setup --host agy` |
| Gemini CLI | experimental | `--host gemini` (or `--host gemini-cli`) → `~/.gemini/skills/gstack-*/` | ask for `gstack-office-hours` | advisory, not blocked | Codex CLI, signed in | `./setup --host gemini` |
| Slate | instruction-only | `--host slate` (points at the Claude install; Slate reads `.claude/skills`) | `/office-hours` via the Claude install | advisory, not blocked | — | `./setup --host claude` |
| OpenClaw | experimental | `--host openclaw` (five task skills and one `gstack` router skill in OpenClaw's skills folder; automatic when setup runs inside OpenClaw; ACP route in [docs/OPENCLAW.md](docs/OPENCLAW.md)) | ask for the task; the agent opens the matching task skill or the `gstack` router | advisory, not blocked | — | `./setup --host openclaw` |
| Hermes | experimental | `--host hermes` (every skill in `$HERMES_HOME/skills/gstack`; automatic when setup runs inside Hermes) | ask for the task, or `/gstack-review` | advisory, not blocked | — | `./setup --host hermes` |
| GBrain (mod) | instruction-only | `--host gbrain` (brain-aware variants ship from the GBrain repo) | — | advisory, not blocked | — | — |

Per-host notes (agent harnesses, Copilot, Antigravity, Gemini CLI, OpenClaw and ClawHub, the Codex behavioral profile and model tiers, outside-review providers, the design binary's models) are in [docs/hosts.md](docs/hosts.md). Any rules-reading agent (Zed, Amp, Jules) can use the 2KB [agents digest](agents-digest/gstack-AGENTS.md) with no install. Adding a host: [docs/ADDING_A_HOST.md](docs/ADDING_A_HOST.md).

## See it work

```
You:    I want to build a daily briefing app for my calendar.
You:    /office-hours
Claude: [asks about the pain — specific examples, not hypotheticals]

You:    Multiple Google calendars, events with stale info, wrong locations.
        Prep takes forever and the results aren't good enough...

Claude: I'm going to push back on the framing. You said "daily briefing
        app." But what you actually described is a personal chief of
        staff AI.
        [extracts 5 capabilities you didn't realize you were describing]
        [challenges 4 premises — you agree, disagree, or adjust]
        [generates 3 implementation approaches with effort estimates]
        RECOMMENDATION: Ship the narrowest wedge tomorrow, learn from
        real usage. The full vision is a 3-month project — start with
        the daily briefing that actually works.
        [writes design doc → feeds into downstream skills automatically]

You:    /plan-ceo-review
        [reads the design doc, challenges scope, runs 10-section review]

You:    /plan-eng-review
        [ASCII diagrams for data flow, state machines, error paths]
        [test matrix, failure modes, security concerns]

You:    Approve plan. Exit plan mode.
        [writes 2,400 lines across 11 files. ~8 minutes.]

You:    /review
        [AUTO-FIXED] 2 issues. [ASK] Race condition → you approve fix.

You:    /qa https://staging.myapp.com
        [opens real browser, clicks through flows, finds and fixes a bug]

You:    /ship
        Tests: 42 → 51 (+9 new). PR: github.com/you/app/pull/42
```

You said "daily briefing app." The agent said "you're building a chief of staff AI" — because it listened to your pain, not your feature request. Eight commands, end to end. That is not a copilot. That is a team.

## The sprint

gstack is a process, not a collection of tools. The skills run in the order a sprint runs:

**Think → Plan → Build → Review → Test → Ship → Reflect**

Each skill feeds into the next. `/office-hours` writes a design doc that `/plan-ceo-review` reads. `/plan-eng-review` writes a test plan that `/qa` picks up. `/review` catches bugs that `/ship` verifies are fixed. Nothing falls through the cracks because every step knows what came before it.

| Skill | Your specialist | What they do |
|-------|----------------|--------------|
| `/office-hours` | **YC Office Hours** | Start here. Six forcing questions that reframe your product before you write code. Pushes back on your framing, challenges premises, generates implementation alternatives. Design doc feeds into every downstream skill. |
| `/plan-ceo-review` | **CEO / Founder** | Rethink the problem. Find the 10-star product hiding inside the request. Four modes: Expansion, Selective Expansion, Hold Scope, Reduction. |
| `/plan-eng-review` | **Eng Manager** | Lock in architecture, data flow, diagrams, edge cases, and tests. Forces hidden assumptions into the open. |
| `/plan-design-review` | **Senior Designer** | Rates each design dimension 0-10, explains what a 10 looks like, then edits the plan to get there. AI Slop detection. Interactive — one AskUserQuestion per design choice. |
| `/plan-devex-review` | **Developer Experience Lead** | Interactive DX review: explores

readme_content: # e2e [e2e](https://e2e.com?utm_source=e2e&utm_medium=github&utm_campaign=readme_intro) is an end-to-end testing framework for web and mobile apps. Describe a goal in natural language and an agent drives the app to reach it. Check the result with locators and assertions in the same test. ```ts // tests/checkout.e2e.ts import { test, expect } from 'e2e'; test('a member upgrades to Pro', async ({ app, agent, screen }) => { await app.open('/settings/billing'); await agent.act('upgrade the workspace to the Pro plan'); await agent.assert('the invoice preview shows a prorated amount'); await expect(screen.getByRole('status')).toContainText('Pro'); }); ``` An agent step that a later assertion verifies records its actions, and the next run replays them with no model calls until the app changes. Tests without agent steps need no model. Bring your own subscription, API key, or local model. ## Quick start ```bash npx e2e init ``` `init` asks for an engine, web or mobile, and a model provider, then writes a config and an example test. The [quickstart](https://e2e.com/docs/quickstart) covers the rest. To see a finished setup in your stack, open [`examples/`](https://github.com/tester-army/e2e/tree/main/examples): Vite, Next.js, Astro, Angular, Expo, SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose, Kotlin Multiplatform, Flutter, and .NET MAUI, each a standalone project with a passing suite. ## Packages ### Core | Package | What it does | | --- | --- | | [`e2e`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/e2e) | The SDK, runner, and CLI. | | [`@e2e-dev/web`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/web) | Browser engine: Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit through Playwright. | | [`@e2e-dev/mobile`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/mobile) | iOS and Android engine: simulators and emulators through agent-device. | | [`@e2e-dev/decision`](https://e2e.com/docs/decision-models) | Decision-model executors for bounded semantic actions and assertions, and `decisionFilter()`, which leaves out the tests a pull request is unlikely to affect. | | [`@e2e-dev/acp`](https://e2e.com/docs/subscriptions#use-your-coding-agent) | Runs agent steps on your own coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) over the Agent Client Protocol. | ### Integrations | Package | What it does | | --- | --- | | [`@e2e-dev/kernel`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/kernel) | Kernel hosted browsers for the web engine. | | [`@e2e-dev/lightpanda`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/lightpanda) | Lightpanda, the open-source headless browser, started per run for the web engine. | | [`@e2e-dev/smol`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/smol) | smol machines browsers for the web engine: by default, each attempt branches a warm Chromium microVM. | | [`@e2e-dev/testmu`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/testmu) | TestMu AI (formerly LambdaTest) hosted Android emulators, iOS simulators, and real devices for the mobile engine, and hosted Chrome and Edge for the web engine. | | [`@e2e-dev/browserstack`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/browserstack) | BrowserStack App Automate real Android and iOS devices for the mobile engine. | | [`@e2e-dev/limrun`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/limrun) | Limrun hosted iOS simulators and Android emulators for mobile tests. | | [`@e2e-dev/eas`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/eas) | Expo Simulators hosted iOS simulators and Android emulators for the mobile engine. | | [`@e2e-dev/github`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@e2e-dev/github) | Reporter that posts results as a pull request comment. | ## Documentation [e2e.com/docs](https://e2e.com/docs). The `e2e` package ships every page, so coding agents can read them offline in `node_modules/e2e/docs`. ## Join us Join us in changing how software gets tested. [We are hiring.](https://e2e.com/careers?utm_source=e2e&utm_medium=github&utm_campaign=readme_hiring) Questions? Ask on [Discord](https://tester.army/discord). Issues are for bugs and feature requests. Want to hack on e2e? See [Contributing](./CONTRIBUTING.md). We prefer an issue or a Discord discussion before a pull request. ## Security Please don't open public issues for security vulnerabilities. Follow [SECURITY.md](./SECURITY.md) and report them to [security@e2e.com](mailto:security@e2e.com). ## Telemetry The CLI sends anonymous usage data, such as which commands and engines run and where runs fail, but no test content, app content, or credentials. Opt out with `npx e2e telemetry disable` or `E2E_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1`. [Telemetry](https://e2e.com/docs/telemetry) lists every field. ## Status > [!NOTE] > e2e is in active development on the way to 1.0. APIs and config can still > change between minor releases.

name: spec-kit
description: 💫 Toolkit to help you get started with SDD or any other process!
readme_content:
🌱 Spec Kit

Build with a spec, fix a bug, or assess an idea — with your coding agent.

English · 简体中文 · 日本語 · 한국어

Spec Kit is an open source toolkit that gives AI coding agents structured processes, reusable templates, and documented outcomes. Start with a ready-made process, customize it, or bring your own. ## Choose your process | What you need | Process | Outcome | | --- | --- | --- | | Build a feature or application | [Spec-Driven Development](#spec-driven-development) | A specification carried through planning, implementation, and convergence | | Diagnose and repair broken behavior | [Bug fixing](#bug-fixing) | An assessed cause, scoped fix, and recorded verification | | Decide whether an idea deserves investment | [Idea assessment](#idea-assessment) | An evidence-backed go, clarify, or stop decision | | Adopt or create a different process | [Your own process](#capabilities) | A process adapted or assembled from reusable primitives | These are independent entry points, not mandatory phases. SDD ships in core; bug fixing and assessment are bundled extensions you install when needed, and the primitives below let you adopt or create other processes. ## Capabilities Spec Kit combines ready-to-use processes with composable mechanisms: | Capability | Spec Kit mechanism | | --- | --- | | Connect to or switch between coding agents | [Integration](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/integrations/index.html) | | Add a command, quality gate, or complete process | [Extension](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/extensions/overview.html) | | Connect a process to an external tool or service | [Extension](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/extensions/overview.html) | | React to coding-agent lifecycle events | [Extension runtime event](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/extensions/api.html#extension-runtime-events) | | Run extension commands before or after Spec Kit commands | [Extension hook](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/extensions/api.html#hook-configuration) | | Adapt templates, commands, terminology, or methodology | [Preset](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/presets/overview.html) | | Enforce organizational or regulatory standards | [Preset](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/presets/overview.html) | | Override a template for one project | [Project-local override](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/how-to/customization.html#project-local-overrides-and-resolution) | | Automate prompts, commands, gates, and shell tasks | [Workflow](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/workflows/overview.html) | | Modify an installed workflow without forking it | [Workflow overlay](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/workflows/overlays.html) | | Add reusable executable behavior to workflows | [Workflow step](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/workflow-steps/developing.html#custom-step-packages) | | Install a curated setup for a role or team | [Bundle](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/bundles/overview.html) | | Discover community components | [Catalog](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/overview/catalogs.html) | | Host a private catalog of approved components | [Catalog](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/overview/catalogs.html) | | Access private catalogs and component downloads | [Authentication](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/reference/authentication.html) | | Work offline or behind a firewall | [Local sources and self-hosted catalogs](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/install/air-gapped.html) | | Inspect which layer supplies a command, template, or script | [Artifact inventory](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/overview/artifacts.html) | Search the active catalogs with commands such as `specify extension search`, `specify preset search`, `specify workflow search`, and `specify bundle search`. Spec Kit includes community catalogs, and organizations can add their own curated sources. Catalog listings are not audits or endorsements, so review community source code before installing or running it. ## Get started You need Python 3.11+, [uv](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/install/uv.html), and a supported AI coding agent on Linux, macOS, or Windows. Run these commands in your terminal to install Spec Kit and create a project. This example uses GitHub Copilot. ```bash uv tool install specify-cli specify init my-project --integration copilot cd my-project ``` After installing the Specify CLI and creating your project, launch your coding agent in the project directory, then choose a process below. For other setups: - [Installation](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/installation.html) for pinned releases, other installers, CI, and troubleshooting. - [Existing projects](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/how-to/existing-projects.html) to start with code you already have. - [Other agents](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/integrations/index.html) for integration keys and [invocation syntax](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/integrations/cli.html#command-invocation). - [Upgrade](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/upgrade.html) to update an existing installation. ## Spec-Driven Development Define what to build and why, then turn the specification into a plan, tasks, and working code. The minimal flow is shown below. Create a constitution once per project and repeat the remaining steps for each feature. Run these skills in your agent's chat, not your terminal, one at a time, reviewing each result before continuing. This example uses GitHub Copilot's default skills syntax. For another agent, use its [equivalent invocation syntax](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/integrations/cli.html#command-invocation). ```text /speckit-constitution Create principles focused on code quality, testing, and maintainability. /speckit-specify Build a photo organizer with albums grouped by date and a tile preview of each album. /speckit-plan Use Vite with vanilla JavaScript. Keep images local and store metadata in SQLite. /speckit-tasks /speckit-implement /speckit-converge ``` Repeat implement and converge until convergence reports `Converged`. For clarification, checklists, and consistency analysis, see the SDD walkthrough. [SDD walkthrough](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/quickstart.html) · [Command reference](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/reference/agentic-sdd.html) ## Bug fixing Assess the cause, fix the bug, and verify the original symptom is resolved. No SDD feature workflow is required first. Install the bug-fixing extension in your terminal, from the project directory: ```bash specify extension add bug ``` Run these skills in your agent's chat, not your terminal, one at a time, reviewing each result before continuing. This example uses GitHub Copilot's default skills syntax. For another agent, use its [equivalent invocation syntax](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/integrations/cli.html#command-invocation). ```text /speckit-bug-assess "Submitting an empty password crashes the login form." slug=login-crash /speckit-bug-fix slug=login-crash /speckit-bug-test slug=login-crash ``` Review the reports in `.specify/bugs/login-crash/`. The final verdict is `verified`, `partial`, or `failed`; only `verified` confirms a successful fix. [Bug-fixing walkthrough](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/guides/bugfix.html) · [Command reference](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/reference/agentic-bugfix.html) ## Idea assessment Gather evidence to decide whether an idea is worth pursuing. No source code or SDD feature workflow is required. Install the assessment extension in your terminal, from the project directory: ```bash specify extension add assess ``` Run these skills in your agent's chat, not your terminal, one at a time, reviewing each result before continuing. This example uses GitHub Copilot's default skills syntax. For another agent, use its [equivalent invocation syntax](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/integrations/cli.html#command-invocation). ```text /speckit-assess-intake "Let users work offline and sync when they reconnect." slug=offline-mode /speckit-assess-research slug=offline-mode /speckit-assess-define slug=offline-mode /speckit-assess-shape slug=offline-mode /speckit-assess-decide slug=offline-mode ``` Review the artifacts in `.specify/assessments/offline-mode/` and the final decision: `go`, `needs-clarification`, or `kill`. Resolve unknowns by editing the existing Markdown artifacts, directly or with your agent, rather than rerunning whole stages. If you choose to build a software idea with a `go` decision, establish a project constitution if needed, then pass the handoff summary from `decision.md` to `/speckit-specify`. Stopping with a documented reason is also a useful outcome. [Assessment walkthrough](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/guides/assessment.html) · [Command reference](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/reference/agentic-assessment.html) ## Customize or bring your own process Customize Spec-Driven Development, bug fixing, or idea assessment to fit your team's standards. Or bring your own process without adopting any of them. Combine the [capabilities above](#capabilities) to match your goal: - Adapt an existing process with a preset, such as requiring regulatory traceability in plans. Use a project-local override for a one-off template change. - Bring your own process by adding its commands through an extension and exposing them to your coding agent through an integration. - Automate commands and checks in a workflow. Use overlays to adapt an installed workflow without forking it, or add custom workflow steps when the built-in types are not enough. - Share a reusable setup by packaging its extensions, presets, workflows, and workflow steps in a bundle. Start with the smallest change that meets your needs; you do not have to replace the whole process. [Customization guide](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/how-to/customization.html) · [Community components and walkthroughs](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/community/overview.html) ## Documentation - [CLI reference](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/index.html#specify-cli) and [process commands](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/reference/agentic-sdd.html#command-overview) - [How-to guides](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/how-to/index.html) for applying Spec Kit to your project work - [SDD philosophy](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/how-to/sdd.html), [fu

[project]
name = "specify-cli"
version = "1.3.2.dev0"
description = "Specify CLI, part of GitHub Spec Kit. A tool to bootstrap your projects for Spec-Driven Development (SDD)."
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = [
    "typer>=0.24.0",
    "click>=8.2.1",
    "rich",
    "readchar",
    "pyyaml>=6.0",
    "packaging>=23.0",
    "pathspec>=0.12.0",
    "json5>=0.13.0",
    "mcp>=2.2.0,<3.0.0",
    "pydantic>=2.13.0,<3.0.0",
    "lark>=1.3.1,<2.0.0",
]

[project.scripts]
specify = "specify_cli:main"

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel]
packages = ["src/specify_cli"]

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel.force-include]
# Bundle core assets so `specify init` works without network access (air-gapped / enterprise)
# Page templates (exclude commands/ — bundled separately below to avoid duplication)
"templates/checklist-template.md" = "specify_cli/core_pack/templates/checklist-template.md"
"templates/constitution-template.md" = "specify_cli/core_pack/templates/constitution-template.md"
"templates/plan-template.md" = "specify_cli/core_pack/templates/plan-template.md"
"templates/spec-template.md" = "specify_cli/core_pack/templates/spec-template.md"
"templates/tasks-template.md" = "specify_cli/core_pack/templates/tasks-template.md"
"templates/vscode-settings.json" = "specify_cli/core_pack/templates/vscode-settings.json"
# Command templates
"templates/commands" = "specify_cli/core_pack/commands"
"scripts/bash" = "specify_cli/core_pack/scripts/bash"
"scripts/powershell" = "specify_cli/core_pack/scripts/powershell"
"scripts/python" = "specify_cli/core_pack/scripts/python"
# Bundled extensions (installable via `specify extension add <name>`)
"extensions/git" = "specify_cli/core_pack/extensions/git"
"extensions/agent-context" = "specify_cli/core_pack/extensions/agent-context"
"extensions/assess" = "specify_cli/core_pack/extensions/assess"
"extensions/bug" = "specify_cli/core_pack/extensions/bug"
"extensions/github" = "specify_cli/core_pack/extensions/github"
# Bundled workflows (`specify init` installs only `speckit`; `bugfix`/`assess` are opt-in via first-party bundles)
"workflows/speckit" = "specify_cli/core_pack/workflows/speckit"
"workflows/bugfix" = "specify_cli/core_pack/workflows/bugfix"
"workflows/assess" = "specify_cli/core_pack/workflows/assess"
# Bundled presets (installable via `specify preset add <name>` or `specify init --preset <name>`)
"presets/lean" = "specify_cli/core_pack/presets/lean"
"presets/constitution-sync" = "specify_cli/core_pack/presets/constitution-sync"
# Bundle catalog snapshots (used for offline discovery)
"bundles/catalog.json" = "specify_cli/core_pack/bundles/catalog.json"
"bundles/catalog.community.json" = "specify_cli/core_pack/bundles/catalog.community.json"

[project.optional-dependencies]
test = [
    "pytest>=7.0",
    "pytest-cov>=4.0",
    "pytest-xdist>=3.0",
]

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
python_files = ["test_*.py"]
python_classes = ["Test*"]
python_functions = ["test_*"]
addopts = [
    "-v",
    "--strict-markers",
    "--tb=short",
]

[tool.coverage.run]
source = ["src"]
omit = ["*/tests/*", "*/__pycache__/*"]

[tool.coverage.report]
precision = 2
show_missing = true
skip_covered = false

[tool.ruff.lint]
# Lock in subprocess security posture: any reintroduction of shell=True
# (or os.system / popen2) must be acknowledged with an explicit `# noqa`
# pointing at the rule, making the deviation visible in review.
extend-select = [
    "S602",  # subprocess-popen-with-shell-equals-true
    "S604",  # call-with-shell-equals-true
    "S605",  # start-process-with-a-shell
]

name: gpui-kit
description: Rust GUI components for building fantastic cross-platform desktop application by using GPUI.
readme_content:
GPUI Kit

[English](./README.md) | [简体中文](./README.zh-CN.md) [![Build Status](https://github.com/longbridge/gpui-kit/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/longbridge/gpui-kit/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Docs](https://docs.rs/gpui-kit/badge.svg)](https://docs.rs/gpui-kit/) [![Crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/gpui-kit.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/gpui-kit) Build fantastic, high-performance desktop apps with Rust and GPUI. GPUI Kit is a comprehensive Rust desktop application framework. It combines a production-ready UI system with application-grade data, layout, and editing capabilities, all built on a reusable foundation of behavior, state, and infrastructure. GPUI Kit ships 75+ documented components and primitives, WebAssembly support, AccessKit accessibility, UI integration testing, and an optional JavaScript extension runtime. Documentation: ```text gpui-kit The one crate applications depend on ├── gpui-base Unstyled behavior, state, and infrastructure └── gpui-component GPUI Component: the complete styled UI system ``` `gpui-kit` pins the matching GPUI release and re-exports GPUI, base, component, and assets, so a Rust application lists a single dependency. JavaScript extension hosts add `gpui-shell` separately; its default `components` feature supplies the styled catalog. See the [executable application recipe and AI-assisted development acceptance checks](examples/ai_recipes/README.md) for a tested starting point and verification commands. ## Features - **75+ Components and Primitives**: Forms, navigation, overlays, data display, editing, feedback, and layout, with polished interactions and productive defaults. - **Production Ready**: Used to build Longbridge Pro from day one and continuously refined in a publicly shipped commercial desktop application. - **WebAssembly**: Run applications and the same component showcases on the web with `wasm32-unknown-unknown`. - **Accessibility**: AccessKit roles, names, states, relationships, and actions are built into the interaction layer and covered by tests. - **UI Integration Testing**: Render real components in headless windows, drive pointer and keyboard input, and assert state, focus, layout, and accessibility. - **Native Feel**: Modern controls inspired by macOS and Windows, backed by semantic themes and multiple sizes. - **120 FPS**: GPU-accelerated interfaces that remain smooth under load. - **Data Tables**: Virtual scrolling, fixed and resizable columns, sorting, and cell selection across hundreds of thousands of rows. - **Virtual Lists**: Render only the visible range, including lists whose items have different sizes. - **Code Editor**: Stable performance at 200K lines with Tree-sitter highlighting and LSP diagnostics, completion, and hover. - **Dock Layout**: Resizable panels, draggable tabs, nested splits, and edge docks — all serializable. - **Rich Content**: Native Markdown and HTML rendering, syntax highlighting, and built-in charts. - **Design Freedom**: Use the complete visual system or build your own on the behavior and infrastructure in `gpui-base`. - **JavaScript Extensions**: `gpui-shell` lets a shipped Rust host load panels and business logic as scripts, with every capability granted explicitly. - **Cross Platform**: Ship one Rust codebase to macOS, Windows, and Linux. ## Framework Architecture ### Three layers. One ecosystem. Use `gpui-component` to keep the application coherent with one complete visual and interaction system. Use `gpui-base` when your product needs to create and own that system itself. Use `gpui-shell` when the application should be extensible in JavaScript after it ships. | **`gpui-component`** | **`gpui-base`** | **`gpui-shell`** | | -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | | Complete, styled components | Unstyled behavior and infrastructure | JavaScript runtime hosted by Rust | | Productive defaults with theming | Full control over structure and visual design | Capabilities granted one at a time | | Best for building applications | Best for building design systems | Best for plugins and scripted applications | ```text APPLICATION │ ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ │ gpui-component │ │ Your Design │ │ gpui-shell │ │ Styled UI │ │ System │ │ JS extensions │ └────────┬─────────┘ └────────┬─────────┘ └────────┬─────────┘ │ │ │ └────────────────────┼────────────────────┘ ▼ ┌──────────────────┐ │ gpui-base │ │ Behavior · State │ │ Infrastructure │ └────────┬─────────┘ ▼ GPUI ``` > **Behavior belongs to the foundation. Presentation belongs to the application.** Use **`gpui-component`** when you want polished controls ready to ship. Build on **`gpui-base`** when your application should own its component source, layout, styling, and motion while reusing difficult interaction behavior. Add **`gpui-shell`** when contributors should extend the product without a fork or a release. The layering follows the same separation that makes the [shadcn](https://ui.shadcn.com) ecosystem flexible: | GPUI Kit ecosystem | Web ecosystem | | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------- | | GPUI | HTML + Tailwind CSS | | [`gpui-base`](crates/base/README.md) | [Base UI](https://base-ui.com) | | `gpui-component` | shadcn's styled component layer | [Explore the architecture →](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) ## Showcase GPUI Kit has powered [Longbridge Pro](https://longbridge.com/desktop) from day one. The framework is extracted from the demands of a publicly shipped commercial desktop application rather than designed in isolation. > **GPUI provides the rendering foundation. Longbridge provides the production foundation.** ## Usage ```toml [dependencies] gpui-kit = "0.7" ``` `gpui-kit` always brings in GPUI and `gpui-base`; `gpui-component` and the default icon set are on by default. Turn default features off to keep only the layers you use. The `gpui-component` features (`inspector`, `decimal`, `tree-sitter`, and each `tree-sitter-`) are available under the same names. ### GPUI Fast Enable the optional `gpui-fast` feature to select [GPUI Fast](https://github.com/longbridge/gpui-fast) for the core, native platforms, WebAssembly, and every enabled Kit layer: ```toml [dependencies] gpui-kit = { version = "0.7", features = ["gpui-fast"] } ``` Keep the same imports, initialization, and test macros; no application `[patch]` or crate alias is needed. The default backend remains the pinned upstream GPUI snapshot. Cargo features are additive, so upstream packages still compile when Fast is selected. See [Getting Started](https://gpui-kit.com/docs/getting-started) for feature combinations and comparison commands. ### Basic Example ```rs use gpui_kit::component::button::*; use gpui_kit::component::*; use gpui_kit::*; pub struct HelloWorld; impl Render for HelloWorld { fn render(&mut self, _: &mut Window, _: &mut Context) -> impl IntoElement { div() .v_flex() .gap_2() .size_full() .items_center() .justify_center() .child("Hello, World!") .child( Button::new("ok") .primary() .label("Let's Go!") .on_click(|_, _, _| println!("Clicked!")), ) } } fn main() { gpui_kit::application().run(move |cx| { // This must be called before using any GPUI Component features. gpui_kit::init(cx); gpui_kit::open_window(WindowOptions::default(), cx, |_, cx| { cx.new(|_| HelloWorld) }) .expect("Failed to open window"); }); } ``` `gpui_kit::open_window` is the application window entry point and always mounts a Base `Root`. Component initialization registers styled window facilities; Cargo features do not select a different root type. ### Icons The default `assets` feature bundles the [Lucide](https://lucide.dev) icon set as `gpui-kit-assets`; pass it to the application with `gpui_kit::application().with_assets(gpui_kit::assets::Assets)`. To ship your own icons instead, leave that feature out and name the SVG files as defined in [IconName](https://github.com/longbridge/gpui-kit/blob/main/crates/component/src/icon.rs#L86). ## Skills for AI Coding Agents Install the GPUI Kit skills for your AI coding agent (Cursor, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex, etc.): ```bash npx skills add longbridge/gpui-kit ``` | Skill | Description | | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `gpui-kit` | Setup, component catalog, usage patterns, GPUI mechanics (elements, entities, async, focus, actions, tests), and the Coding Guides. | | `gpui-kit-design-guides` | The Design Guides: layout, spacing, hierarchy, interaction states, overlays, and interface copy. | ## Development ### Desktop Gallery (Story) The `story` crate is a gallery application that showcases all available components. Run it with: ```bash cargo run ``` ### Examples Some larger examples reuse the `story` gallery components and run as standalone packages: ```bash # Dock layout system (panels, split views, tabs) cargo run -p example-dock # Markdown rendering cargo run -p example-markdown # HTML rendering cargo run -p example-html ``` The `examples` directory also contains standalone examples, each focused on a single feature. Each example is a separate crate, run them with `cargo run -p `: ```bash # Code editor with LSP support and syntax highlighting cargo run -p example-editor # Basic hello world cargo run -p hello_world # System monitor (real-time charts with CPU/memory data) cargo run -p system_monitor # Window title customization cargo run -p window_title ``` Check out [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for more details. ## Compare to others See the [comparison with Iced, egui and Qt 6](https://gpui-kit.com/docs/comparison) on the site. ## Related project: Native Shell [Native Shell](https://nsh.dev) ([source](https://github.com/longbridge/native-shell)) is a sibling project that lets AI generate UI and renders it natively on iOS, Android, Linux (GTK) and macOS (AppKit). Its GPUI desktop backend is in development and will be built on GPUI Kit. ## License Software source and documentation code examples: [Apache-2.0](LICENSE-APACHE). name: figma-console-mcp
description: Your design system as an API. Connect AI to Figma for extraction, creation, and debugging.
readme_content:
# Figma Console MCP Server

[![MCP](https://img.shields.io/badge/MCP-Compatible-blue)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/)
[![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/figma-console-mcp)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/figma-console-mcp)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
[![Documentation](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-docs.figma--console--mcp.southleft.com-0D9488)](https://docs.figma-console-mcp.southleft.com)
[![Sponsor](https://img.shields.io/badge/Sponsor-southleft-ea4aaa?logo=github-sponsors&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/sponsors/southleft)

> **Your design system as an API.** A design-system-focused Model Context Protocol server for Figma. It works in both directions (Figma ⇄ code), **writes to Figma**, and runs **deterministic checks** for design-code parity, accessibility, and design-system health. It hands the AI exact tokens, variants, bindings, and states as structured data rather than prescribing a framework or house style, so generated code follows your team's own stack and conventions.

> **🆕 Shaders, grid and auto layout, OKLCH and P3 color, text wrap and variable fonts (latest v1.46.0):** apply shaders and set their properties by name (`figma_apply_shader`, `figma_list_shaders`), set auto layout or grid layout in one call with CSS-style grid tracks (`figma_set_layout`), use OKLCH, Display P3 and other CSS colors on fills and strokes, and set text wrap (balance, pretty) and variable-font axes with `figma_set_text` (v1.46.0). v1.45 added Motion: animate layers with presets, custom animation styles or keyframes bound to Timing and Easing tokens, export video, and find code layers. [See what's new →](CHANGELOG.md#1460---2026-10-29)

## What is this?

Figma Console MCP connects AI assistants (like Claude) to Figma, enabling:

- **🎨 Design system extraction** - Pull variables, components, and styles
- **🧬 Codebase → design system extraction** - Scan a production codebase, mine its de-facto styling into DTCG tokens with per-token provenance, scaffold a design-system package with a wired Storybook workshop, and gate it with deterministic fidelity evals — then round-trip the tokens into Figma variables (Local Mode)
- **🔁 Bidirectional token sync** - Export Figma variables to DTCG JSON (legacy or 2025.10 dialect) + 9 more formats; push code-side edits back to Figma with full apply — creates, renames, alias re-targeting, and replace-gated deletes. Replaces Style Dictionary and Tokens Studio's export pipeline.
- **📸 Visual debugging** - Take screenshots for context
- **✏️ Design creation** - Create UI components, frames, and layouts directly in Figma — including one-call component-set creation from a variant axes matrix
- **🔧 Variable management** - Create, update, rename, and delete design tokens
- **🕰 Version history & time-series awareness** - List versions, diff snapshots, generate markdown changelogs, trace property/variant introduction via binary-search blame, and fold per-component design + git history into generated component docs
- **⚡ Real-time monitoring** - Watch console logs from the Desktop Bridge plugin
- **📌 FigJam boards** - Create stickies, flowcharts, tables, and code blocks on collaborative boards
- **🎞️ Slides presentations** - Build and manage Figma Slides decks programmatically
- **♿ Accessibility scanning** - 14 WCAG design checks with conformance level tagging, component scorecards, axe-core code scanning, design-to-code parity
- **🔍 Design-code parity & component docs** - Deterministic comparison of a Figma component with its code (visual, spacing, typography, tokens, component API, accessibility), and generated component documentation with per-variant tokens and an optional design + git changelog
- **📋 Design-system health audits** - Lighthouse-style scored audit across naming, tokens, component metadata, accessibility, consistency, and coverage — available as a plain tool for any MCP client (with per-finding auto-fix guidance) and as a visual dashboard app
- **🛡 Cross-MCP identity** - Every tool response carries `_mcp: "figma-console-mcp"` and errors are prefixed `[figma-console-mcp]` so attribution stays unambiguous in agents running multiple Figma MCPs
- **☁️ Cloud Write Relay** - Web AI clients (Claude.ai, v0, Replit) can design in Figma via cloud pairing
- **🔄 Four ways to connect** - Remote SSE, Cloud Mode, NPX, or Local Git

---

## ⚡ Quick Start

### Choose Your Setup

**First, decide what you want to do:**

| I want to... | Setup Method | Time |
|--------------|--------------|------|
| **Create and modify designs with AI** | [NPX Setup](#-npx-setup-recommended) (Recommended) | ~10 min |
| **Design from the web** (Claude.ai, v0, Replit, Lovable) | [Cloud Mode](#-cloud-mode-web-ai-clients) | ~5 min |
| **Contribute to the project** | [Local Git Setup](#for-contributors-local-git-mode) | ~15 min |
| **Just explore my design data** (read-only) | [Remote SSE](#-remote-sse-read-only-exploration) | ~2 min |

### ⚠️ Important: Capability Differences

| Capability | NPX / Local Git | Cloud Mode | Remote SSE |
|------------|-----------------|------------|------------|
| Read design data | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| **Create components & frames** | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| **Edit existing designs** | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| **Manage design tokens/variables** | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| **FigJam boards (stickies, flowcharts)** | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| Real-time monitoring (console, selection) | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Codebase → design system extraction (`figma_ds_*`) | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Desktop Bridge plugin | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| Requires Node.js | Yes | **No** | No |

> **Bottom line:** Remote SSE is **read-only** until you pair the plugin. **Cloud Mode** unlocks write access (105 tools) from web AI clients without Node.js. NPX/Local Git gives the full 130 tools with real-time monitoring.

---

### 🚀 NPX Setup (Recommended)

**Best for:** Designers who want full AI-assisted design capabilities.

**What you get:** All 130 tools including design creation, variable management, and component instantiation.

#### Prerequisites

- [ ] **Node.js 18+** — Check with `node --version` ([Download](https://nodejs.org))
- [ ] **Figma Desktop** installed (not just the web app)
- [ ] **An MCP client** (Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Claude Desktop, etc.)

#### Step 1: Get Your Figma Token

1. Go to [Manage personal access tokens](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/articles/8085703771159-Manage-personal-access-tokens) in Figma Help
2. Follow the steps to **create a new personal access token**
3. Enter description: `Figma Console MCP`
4. Set scopes (all Read unless noted): **File content**, **File versions**, **Library content**, **Library assets**, **Comments** (Read and write), **Current user**, and **Variables** (Enterprise only, optional). See [why each is needed](https://docs.figma-console-mcp.southleft.com/setup#step-1-get-your-figma-token-2-min)
5. **Copy the token** — you won't see it again! (starts with `figd_`)

#### Step 2: Configure Your MCP Client

**Claude Code (CLI):**
```bash
claude mcp add figma-console -s user -e FIGMA_ACCESS_TOKEN=figd_YOUR_TOKEN_HERE -e ENABLE_MCP_APPS=true -- npx -y figma-console-mcp@latest
```

**OpenAI Codex (CLI):**
```bash
codex mcp add figma-console --env FIGMA_ACCESS_TOKEN=figd_YOUR_TOKEN_HERE --env ENABLE_MCP_APPS=true -- npx -y figma-console-mcp@latest
```
Then set `startup_timeout_sec = 60` and `tool_timeout_sec = 300` for it in `~/.codex/config.toml` (Codex's 10 s / 60 s defaults are too short). The Codex app and IDE extension share this config. [Full Codex setup →](https://docs.figma-console-mcp.southleft.com/setup#-openai-codex)

**Gemini CLI:**
```bash
gemini mcp add -s user -e FIGMA_ACCESS_TOKEN=figd_YOUR_TOKEN_HERE -e ENABLE_MCP_APPS=true figma-console npx -y figma-console-mcp@latest
```

**Google Antigravity (IDE, CLI, app):** add the JSON below to `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json`, plus `"timeoutSeconds": 300` in the server entry. [Full Antigravity setup →](https://docs.figma-console-mcp.southleft.com/setup#-google-antigravity)

**Cursor / Windsurf / Claude Desktop:**

Add to your MCP config file (see [Where to find your config file](#-where-to-find-your-config-file) below):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "figma-console": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "figma-console-mcp@latest"],
      "env": {
        "FIGMA_ACCESS_TOKEN": "figd_YOUR_TOKEN_HERE",
        "ENABLE_MCP_APPS": "true"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

#### 📂 Where to Find Your Config File

If you're not sure where to put the JSON configuration above, here's where each app stores its MCP config:

| App | macOS | Windows |
|-----|-------|---------|
| **Claude Desktop** | `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json` | `%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json` |
| **Claude Code (CLI)** | `~/.claude.json` | `%USERPROFILE%\.claude.json` |
| **Cursor** | `~/.cursor/mcp.json` | `%USERPROFILE%\.cursor\mcp.json` |
| **Windsurf** | `~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json` | `%USERPROFILE%\.codeium\windsurf\mcp_config.json` |
| **OpenAI Codex** (app, CLI, IDE) | `~/.codex/config.toml` (TOML, [see format](https://docs.figma-console-mcp.southleft.com/setup#-openai-codex)) | `%USERPROFILE%\.codex\config.toml` |
| **Gemini CLI** | `~/.gemini/settings.json` | `%USERPROFILE%\.gemini\settings.json` |
| **Google Antigravity** (IDE, CLI, app) | `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json` | `%USERPROFILE%\.gemini\config\mcp_config.json` |

> **Tip for designers:** The `~` symbol means your **home folder**. On macOS, that's `/Users/YourName/`. On Windows, it's `C:\Users\YourName\`. You can open these files in any text editor — even TextEdit or Notepad.
>
> **Can't find the file?** If it doesn't exist yet, create it. The app will pick it up on its next restart. Make sure the entire file is valid JSON (watch for missing commas or brackets).
>
> **Claude Code users:** You can skip manual editing entirely. Just run the `claude mcp add` command above and it handles everything for you.

#### Step 3: Connect to Figma Desktop

**Desktop Bridge Plugin:**
1. Open Figma Desktop normally (no special flags needed) and open a file
2. Go to **Plugins → Development → Import plugin from manifest...**
3. Select `~/.figma-console-mcp/plugin/manifest.json` (stable path, auto-created by the MCP server). Run `npx figma-console-mcp --print-path` to print the exact path for your machine.
4. Run the plugin in your Figma file — it scans ports 9223–9232 and connects automatically to your running MCP server

> **Can't see the folder in the import dialog?** `.figma-console-mcp` starts with a dot, so macOS hides it. In the dialog, press **⌘⇧G** and paste the path (or press **⌘⇧.** to show hidden files). On Windows the folder is visible as normal.

> **Heads-up on plugin updates.** Figma caches plugin files (`code.js` and `ui.html`) at the application level. The MCP server refreshes the files at `~/.figma-console-mcp/plugin/` on every startup, but Figma keeps using its cached copy until you re-import the manifest.
>
> **Re-importing is _required_ only when a release notes entry says so** — typically when the plugin adds a new method the server needs (e.g. v1.22.4, v1.10.0). The plugin files last changed in v1.41.5; if your imported plugin predates that, re-import once. The plugin shows an update banner when the server bundles a newer plugin than the one running. For most upgrades the new server stays wire-compatible with the previous plugin, and re-importing is **optional**: you'll still get every functional change, just not the cosmetic plugin-side touches (status-pill copy, `pluginVersion` reporting).
>
> When you do re-import: Plugins → Manage plugins → re-import `~/.figma-console-mcp/plugin/manifest.json`. The stable path never changes, so it's a one-click step.

#### Step 4: Restart Your MCP Client

Restart your MCP client to load the new configuration.
